intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the section exercises in pencil, check yourself against the recall questions, and write your own notes in the margins.

sections.title: What Is Political Economy?
sections.big_idea: Good economics is not enough, because every reform **redistributes**, and the losers are usually organised.
in_plain_words: Economics asks how scarce resources are allocated and politics asks who holds power. Political economy puts them in one system: markets are shaped by rules, and rules by power. Lasswell's question, who gets what, when and how, is answered by every budget line, subsidy, tariff, posting and licence.

That is why technically sound reforms stall. The losers are few, lose a lot each and are already organised, while the winners are many, gain a little and rarely mobilise. **Concentrated losses beat diffuse gains.** Keep explaining (positive) apart from judging (normative), and pick the level, from household to global, that fits your problem.

right.title: Political economy adds
items: Who benefits from the current one?

key_terms.meaning: How political power and economic forces decide who gets what.
Asks what is and why.
Asks what ought to be.
A large cost falling on a few identifiable people.
A small benefit spread across many.
Micro, meso, macro and global.

worked_example.title: Read decisions as distribution
worked_example.setup: Take five routine administrative decisions and say what each one decides.
steps: A budget line decides who gets money.
A subsidy decides which activity is cheap.
A tariff decides which producers are protected.
A posting decides who holds discretion, and a licence decides who may enter.
Add the extra question: who decided, and by what procedure?
worked_example.answer: Each routine decision answers Lasswell, so each has winners, losers and a procedure to examine.

mistakes: Calling a stalled reform a lack of political will without asking whose will.
Treating a technically correct recommendation as a feasible one.
Mixing normative claims into an explanation of why a subsidy persists.
Analysing at the national level when the problem sits in one district's scheme.

recall.q: Who said politics is who gets what, when, how, and when?
recall.a: Harold Lasswell, 1936.

recall.q: Why do losers usually win the politics?
recall.a: They are few, lose a lot each and are organised, while winners are dispersed and gain little each.

recall.q: What two tasks does the asymmetry imply?
recall.a: Organise the winners or compensate the losers.

recall.q: What is the difference between a positive and a normative question?
recall.a: A positive question asks what is and why. A normative question asks what ought to be.

recall.q: Why does the deck say political economy is a practitioner's tool?
recall.a: It diagnoses why reforms stall, maps who can block, and finds feasible entry points.

sections.title: Classical Roots
sections.big_idea: Smith, Ricardo and Marx are **three lenses** that arguments still use.
in_plain_words: Economics began as political economy, the study of how nations produce and distribute wealth, inseparable from the state. The late nineteenth century renaming narrowed the lens. The recent revival returns to the founders' wider question.

Smith's invisible hand needs real competition and he warned against monopoly. Ricardo's comparative advantage shows gains from trade but is silent on who bears the losses. Marx adds class and surplus value, and asks whose interest an idea serves. **A modern trade argument runs on Ricardo, a competition argument on Smith, and who captures the gains on Marx.**

diagram.caption: from a broad question to a narrow discipline

key_terms.meaning: Self-interest serving society under real competition.
Gains from trade by specialising in what one does relatively best.
Value labour creates beyond wages, in Marx the source of profit.
Can make a particular interest look like the common good.
Specialisation that raises output, limited by the extent of the market.

worked_example.title: Which lens is this argument using?
worked_example.setup: A colleague offers three claims. Name the thinker each stands on.
steps: 'Opening this sector to entrants will lower prices': competition, so Smith.
'Both countries gain if each specialises': comparative advantage, so Ricardo.
'Who captures the gains from this policy consensus?': material interest and class, so Marx.
For each, ask what the lens assumes and what it leaves out.
worked_example.answer: Smith, Ricardo and Marx in that order; knowing the lens shows the argument's assumptions.

mistakes: Treating Smith as a prophet of greed and ignoring his warnings about monopoly.
Reading comparative advantage as saying everyone within a country gains.
Assuming adjustment to trade is costless.
Rejecting Marx's tools because you reject his political programme.

recall.q: In what year did Smith publish The Wealth of Nations?
What does comparative advantage say nothing about?
recall.a: How the gains are shared or who bears the losses.

recall.q: What is surplus value?
recall.a: The value created by labour beyond what is paid in wages.

recall.q: What does the invisible hand depend on?
recall.a: Real competition and fair rules.

recall.q: What is the most portable Marxian tool?
recall.a: Asking who benefits when an idea is taken as obvious.

sections.title: The State & the Market
sections.big_idea: Markets and states **need each other**, and both fail in predictable ways.
in_plain_words: The lazy debate sets market against state. There is no market without a state to define property, enforce contracts and issue money, so the real question is which does what in this setting. Markets fail through public goods, externalities, information gaps, monopoly power and missing markets. The state has five roles and can fail too.

Polanyi adds that treating land, labour and money as ordinary commodities is a radical experiment. Markets are embedded in society, and each push to marketise provokes a counter-movement. **Plan for the double movement instead of treating backlash as an obstacle.**

levels.label: Redistribute
levels.sub: fails when the tax base is narrow

levels.label: Stabilise
levels.sub: fails when fiscal space is gone

diagram.caption: five roles of the state and how each fails

key_terms.meaning: Under-supplied because free-riders cannot be excluded.
A cost or benefit spilling onto others.
Polanyi's land, labour and money.
Economic activity sits inside social relations and norms.
Market expansion provokes demands for protection.
Capture, missing information, weak capacity, officials' incentives.

worked_example.title: Diagnose the failure
worked_example.setup: Classify four South Asian cases using the market-failure table.
steps: Rural roads and flood defence: public goods.
Groundwater depletion and stubble burning: externalities.
Mandi intermediaries and input dealers: market power.
Crop insurance for smallholders: a missing market.
worked_example.answer: Public goods, externalities, market power and a missing market, and each has someone who profits from the failure.

mistakes: Framing the choice as market or state, which the deck calls a category error.
Assuming state action fixes a market failure automatically.
Reading backlash as 'populism' and nothing more.
Designing for anonymous strangers when the market runs on caste, kin and credit relationships.

recall.q: Name the five market failures.
recall.a: Public goods, externalities, information gaps, monopoly power and missing markets.

recall.q: What are the three fictitious commodities?
recall.a: Land, labour and money.

recall.q: What is the double movement?
recall.a: Market expansion provokes counter-movement demanding protection.

recall.q: Which South Asian examples of counter-movement does the deck give?
recall.a: NREGA, the Right to Food and the Forest Rights Act, and the repeal of the 2020 farm laws.

recall.q: Why is groundwater the hardest externality in the region?
recall.a: The externality is invisible, the users are millions and electricity pricing subsidises extraction.

sections.title: Institutions Matter
sections.big_idea: Rules shape incentives, and **informal rules often bind harder** than formal ones.
in_plain_words: The dominant modern answer to why some countries are rich is institutions: the formal and informal rules that shape incentives to invest and cooperate. North calls them the rules of the game, and distinguishes them from organisations, which are the players.

Acemoglu and Robinson contrast inclusive and extractive institutions through the mechanism of creative destruction. The idea is mainstream and contested: it risks tautology, explains traps better than exits, and struggles with China and East Asia. **Reforms that confuse changing a law with changing a norm fail predictably.**

diagram.caption: rules, norms and the players who work them

key_terms.meaning: Humanly devised constraints that structure interaction.
The players: firms, parties, agencies, NGOs.
Broad rights, open entry, constrained executive.
Funnel wealth and power to a narrow elite.
New entrants threaten incumbents, who block them.
Defining good institutions by the outcomes they explain.

worked_example.title: Rules or players?
worked_example.setup: A donor proposes four fixes. Say whether each changes a rule or adds a player.
steps: A new anti-corruption agency adds a player.
A change to electoral rules changes an institution.
A norm about whose turn it is for a posting is an informal institution.
Strengthening an organisation leaves the rules it operates under untouched.
worked_example.answer: Agency: player. Electoral rules: institution. Whose turn: informal institution. Capacity building often targets the wrong layer.

mistakes: Building a new agency to fix a problem rooted in the rules.
Assuming a country score describes variation inside it.
Treating the inclusive versus extractive binary as a full diagnosis.
Changing a law and assuming the norm it runs into has changed.

recall.q: How does North define institutions?
recall.a: The humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction.

recall.q: Which institutions change slowly?
recall.a: Informal ones such as norms, conventions and patronage.

recall.q: What did Acemoglu, Robinson and Johnson win in 2024?
recall.a: The Nobel Prize in Economics.

recall.q: Name two criticisms of the institutions story.
recall.a: Tautology risk, no theory of change, the China and East Asia counter-case, or aggregation.

recall.q: Why does the causal question remain open?
recall.a: Better institutions may cause wealth, wealth may buy institutions, or a third factor may drive both.

sections.title: Collective Action & Public Goods
sections.big_idea: Small, concentrated groups out-organise large ones, so **diffuse winners must be given a reason to act**.
in_plain_words: Olson showed that rational individuals free-ride on shared benefits, so large groups under-provide their own collective goods. Twenty producers with a large stake each organise and win, while a hundred million consumers with a tiny stake do not. Awareness campaigns do not solve this, because it concerns incentives and not apathy.

Fixes work by changing the calculus: selective incentives, coercion, small size or federation, and leaders who bear start-up cost. Hardin described a commons tragedy, but Ostrom showed communities govern commons. **Her eight design principles are rules for cooperation**, the same insight as North's.

diagram.caption: the five fixes in the deck

key_terms.meaning: Enjoying a benefit without paying for it.
A private reward for members only.
Over-use of a shared finite resource.
Penalties that grow with repeat breaches.
Small groups nested into larger structures.
Community managing forest while the department keeps rule-making.

worked_example.title: Why the many lose
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a tariff gives 20 producers ₹200 crore a year and costs 100 million consumers the same total.
steps: Stake per producer: 200 ÷ 20 = 10 crore rupees.
100 million consumers is 10 crore people.
Cost per consumer: 200 ÷ 10 = 20 rupees.
Ten crore rupees each against twenty rupees each decides who organises.
worked_example.answer: ₹10 crore a producer against ₹20 a consumer, so the twenty producers organise and win.

mistakes: Relying on appeals to the common good when no incentive changes.
Treating every commons as open access with no rules.
Assuming the only options are privatising or nationalising.
Designing institutions with no enforcement or only a single penalty nobody applies.

recall.q: Who wrote The Logic of Collective Action and when?
recall.a: Mancur Olson, 1965.

recall.q: Why do small groups out-organise large ones?
recall.a: Shares are large, free-riders are visible and coordination is cheap.

recall.q: What did Ostrom win and when?
recall.a: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, 2009.

recall.q: Which Ostrom principle is most often missing in designed institutions?
recall.a: Graduated sanctions.

recall.q: Why does the deck call SHGs a model that scales?
recall.a: They federate: self-help group to village organisation to block federation.

sections.title: Rents, Corruption & State Capture
sections.big_idea: Rents come from **artificial scarcity**, and the strongest cure is removing the scarcity and the discretion around it.
in_plain_words: Economic rent is income above what keeps a resource in use. Rent-seeking spends resources to capture it, and the waste includes the competition for the transfer. The pre-1991 Licence Raj shows how permits for capacity and imports made licences valuable and sent entrepreneurs to ministries.

Corruption comes in five types with different remedies, and state capture writes the rules themselves. Elite capture defeats flawless rules, and patronage and clientelism fill gaps left by weak capacity. **Removing discretion works earlier in the chain than enforcement and does not need honest enforcers.**

diagram.caption: the Licence Raj as a rent-seeking chain

key_terms.meaning: Income above what keeps a resource in use.
Spending resources to capture an unearned share.
Private interests shape the rules themselves.
Local powerful groups divert benefits meant for the poor.
Jobs and contracts as favours for loyalty.
A standing exchange of goods for votes.

worked_example.title: Type and remedy
worked_example.setup: Match each case to a type of corruption and a remedy from the deck's table.
steps: Speed money for a certificate: petty; remove discretion or digitise.
A rigged mega-contract: grand; transparency and competitive process.
An inspector demands a cut: bureaucratic; fewer approvals and clear rules.
Donations for policy: political; party finance reform.
A law written for one firm: state capture, legal on its face.
worked_example.answer: Petty, grand, bureaucratic, political and capture, each with a different remedy.

mistakes: Treating all rent as bad, when a conditional learning rent may buy capability.
Expecting one anti-corruption agency to address every type.
Looking for violations when the problem is a lawful rule written for one interest.
Replacing clientelism with moral appeals instead of making the rule-based route work.

recall.q: What is the difference between ordinary corruption and state capture?
recall.a: Ordinary corruption breaks the rule. Capture writes the rule.

recall.q: What did Tullock add about rent-seeking waste?
recall.a: It includes the resources spent competing for the transfer.

recall.q: Which measure is the single most effective against elite capture?
recall.a: Public reading of beneficiary lists, the core of the social audit.

recall.q: What does DBT attack in political-economy terms?
recall.a: The intermediaries who lived off the leakage.

recall.q: Which rent test does the deck give?
recall.a: Whether the rent is conditional on performance.

sections.title: The Political Economy of Development
sections.big_idea: Late developers caught up with states that could **impose conditions on business and enforce them**.
in_plain_words: Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and later China did not win with smaller states. They had developmental states: capable, relatively autonomous bureaucracies that tied cheap credit and protection to verifiable export targets. Subsidy was a contract and underperformers lost support.

Evans calls the balance embedded autonomy: close enough to business to know, distant enough to say no. Resource rents can detach rulers from citizens, and premature deindustrialisation narrows the factory route. **South Asia has often had close ties without the reciprocal conditions.**

key_terms.meaning: Steers transformation through a capable, autonomous bureaucracy.
Support tied to performance, withdrawn if missed.
Connected enough to know, autonomous enough to discipline.
Resource-rich countries often grow slower and govern worse.
A currency boom makes other exports uncompetitive.
Manufacturing peaks at a much lower income.

worked_example.title: Too autonomous, too embedded, or balanced?
worked_example.setup: Place three states using Evans's table.
steps: A bureaucracy with no information about industry: too autonomous; policy misses the mark.
An agency whose policy serves incumbents: too embedded; captured.
A bureaucracy informed and independent: embedded autonomy; policy disciplines.
Check the verifiable condition: can the recipient lobby its way past the target?
worked_example.answer: Too autonomous, too embedded, and embedded autonomy; an unverifiable target would drift towards the second.

mistakes: Concluding that successful late developers had smaller states.
Copying the policy list without the capability that made it work.
Treating subsidies as rent-seeking when the state can discipline recipients.
Treating the resource-curse pattern as established data when the chart is schematic.

recall.q: Who documented the developmental state in Japan, Korea and Taiwan?
recall.a: Chalmers Johnson, Alice Amsden and Robert Wade.

recall.q: Why did export targets work as a discipline?
recall.a: They were externally verifiable, so a firm could not lobby a foreign customer.

recall.q: What are the three resource-curse mechanisms listed on the chart slide?
recall.a: Rents finance the state without taxing citizens, a currency boom hurts other exports, and the prize fuels conflict.

recall.q: Which countries escaped the curse?
recall.a: Norway and Botswana, because institutions came before the resource.

recall.q: What does Rodrik's observation imply for South Asia?
recall.a: The standard route of moving workers from farms to factories may not be available at the same scale.

sections.title: Political Settlements & Power
sections.big_idea: Institutions survive only if they are **compatible with how power is distributed**.
in_plain_words: Donors export independent regulators and anti-corruption agencies and watch them wither, because a new rule grafted onto an unchanged balance of power loses to the power. Khan's political settlement is that underlying balance, and holding power is a group's capacity to benefit itself in conflict.

Power, institutions and outcomes form a slow loop in which outcomes reshape power, so settlements do shift. Informal rules often override formal ones. **Work with the settlement: choose compatible reforms, shift the balance gradually, build the constituency first, and name the trade-off.**

key_terms.meaning: The balance of power between groups and the institutions compatible with it.
A group's capacity to benefit itself in conflict.
Unwritten norm that often overrides the statute.
Form copied, function absent.
Power concentrated or contested, with short horizons.

worked_example.title: Test a reform for compatibility
worked_example.setup: A government plans to strengthen a regulator. Apply the deck's anatomy of a stalled reform.
steps: What does the reform aim to do? Strengthen a regulator.
What does the settlement look like? It favours the firms regulated.
What follows? The regulator is captured, or starved or staffed loyally.
Check compatibility: who must accept a loss, and can they impose costs if they refuse?
Choose a compatible step or a gradual shift in the balance.
worked_example.answer: The reform is technically fine and politically exposed, so redesign it around holding power and a compatible first step.

mistakes: Reading reform failure as an implementation problem when the rule conflicts with the power distribution.
Mapping formal authority and missing the holding power of groups that can disrupt.
Assuming digitisation removes discretion when it often relocates it.
Working with an unjust settlement without naming the trade-off.

recall.q: Who developed the political settlement idea?
recall.a: Mushtaq Khan.

recall.q: What can give a group holding power?
recall.a: Organisation, wealth, numbers or capacity for disruption.

recall.q: Why does the feedback arrow matter?
recall.a: It shows outcomes change the distribution of power, so settlements shift.

recall.q: What do broad settlements allow?
recall.a: Credible long-term commitments and discipline over rent recipients.

recall.q: Name two informal rules that override formal ones.
recall.a: Bribe norms over the fee schedule, and caste hierarchy over equal access provisions.

sections.title: Political Economy Analysis in Practice
sections.big_idea: PEA is useful only when it **changes a design decision**, and it starts from a concrete problem.
in_plain_words: Political Economy Analysis maps interests and power and finds feasible entry points. It became a standard donor product in the 2000s and produced shelf-ware before the shift to problem-driven work. Start from 'teachers absent three days a week here' and leave 'weak governance' behind.

The structures, institutions and actors frame tells you where effort works inside a project horizon: structures take decades, institutions years, actors now. Thinking and Working Politically makes it continuous. **Use PEA to find feasible action and not as an excuse for paralysis.**

diagram.caption: top layer: engage now; bottom layer: decades

key_terms.meaning: A structured way to understand how power and interests shape a problem.
Starts from one concrete problem and ends with an entry point.
Structures, institutions, actors.
Thinking and Working Politically: continuous reading and adaptation.
A study that sits unread.

worked_example.title: Sharpen the problem and place the layers
worked_example.setup: A team writes 'weak governance' in its draft.
steps: Replace it with a place, a group and an observable: 'frontline workers absent three days a week here'.
Structures: the district's geography and social structure. Account for them.
Institutions: the formal posting rule and the informal rule about whose turn it is.
Actors: the staff, the supervisors and the postings authority; engage them.
worked_example.answer: A sharp problem plus the three layers gives a map the team can act on.

mistakes: Annexing a PEA to an unchanged programme document.
Spending most pages on structures, the layer you cannot change.
Using PEA to justify a plan the funder had already chosen.
Letting a power map go stale between reviews.

recall.q: What does PEA not produce?
recall.a: A prediction, a guarantee or a neutral analysis.

recall.q: Who is associated with the shift to problem-driven PEA?
recall.a: David Booth and others at ODI.

recall.q: Which layer is the most operational?
recall.a: Actors.

recall.q: Name two misuses of PEA and their guards.
recall.a: Doing nothing, guarded by requiring an entry point; justifying a pre-existing plan, guarded by analysis before design.

recall.q: What is the practical minimum for TWP?
recall.a: A standing agenda item at every review on what has changed politically.

sections.title: Applying PEA
sections.big_idea: Name the problem, map the actors, trace their incentives, and find **a feasible entry point**.
in_plain_words: Applied PEA runs in four steps. Map interests against power and choose a tactic by quadrant: champions are given what they need, blockers are neutralised, allies are built up. Follow the incentives and not the org chart, because systems reward reporting when targets are not verified.

Entry points come from aligned interests, a champion, a window or a small win. Organise the diffuse winners and make hidden costs visible. **Best practice travels badly as isomorphic mimicry**, and PDIA starts from local problems and takes small steps.

diagram.caption: the four steps of applied PEA

key_terms.meaning: Actors plotted by power and stance.
A feasible place to start: aligned interests, champion, window or small win.
Adopting the appearance of capable institutions without the function.
Problem-driven iterative adaptation.
A crisis, election or scandal that shifts the balance.

worked_example.title: Place the pensions actors
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's illustrative case where pensions do not reach the elderly poor in a district.
steps: Middlemen who take a cut: powerful and opposed, so blockers.
A reformist district officer: powerful and supportive, so a champion.
Elderly beneficiaries and elders: weak and supportive, so allies to build.
Entry point: direct transfer plus a public list, which cuts the middleman and arms the poor.
worked_example.answer: Blockers, champion and allies, with a direct transfer and a public list as the first step.

mistakes: Using vague problem statements such as weak governance or corruption.
Reading the incentive as the job description.
Waiting for a window without having the analysis ready.
Importing a Rwanda or Korea template without checking the settlement.

recall.q: What are the four steps of applied PEA?
recall.a: Name the problem, map the actors, trace interests and incentives, find a feasible entry point.

recall.q: What is the strategy for a powerful, opposed actor?
recall.a: Neutralise, compensate or avoid.

recall.q: Who coined isomorphic mimicry?
recall.a: Pritchett, Woolcock and Andrews.

recall.q: What is PDIA's main obstacle?
recall.a: Funding, since iteration is hard to write into a fixed logframe.

recall.q: What is the strategy for weak and opposed actors?
recall.a: Watch them as latent foes, for any change in their power.

sections.title: India / South Asia & Further Reading
sections.big_idea: India is a **paradox of reach and delivery**, and caste, federalism and competition shape every analysis.
in_plain_words: India combines a durable democracy with a vast state that delivers unevenly, deep social cleavages and federal bargaining. Bardhan saw three dominant proprietary classes blocking each other, and Kohli separates pro-business from pro-market. Caste operates as an economic institution.

Welfare politics has expanded transfers because they are attributable, while a functioning school is diffuse. The wider region offers four settlements in similar conditions. **State-level variation is the analytical opportunity**, and the reading list gives you the sources behind each idea.

key_terms.meaning: Bardhan: capitalists, rich farmers, the professional elite.
Favours existing firms and their profits.
Favours competition and entry.
Mediates tax shares between Centre and states.
Shared body for indirect taxation.
A standing exchange of goods for votes.

worked_example.title: Match class to claim
worked_example.setup: Use Bardhan's three classes and what each claims from the state.
steps: Industrial capitalists: protection, licences and credit.
Rich farmers: input subsidies, price support and no land tax.
Professionals in the state: employment, discretion and status.
None could dominate and each could veto, so subsidies spread across all three.
worked_example.answer: Each class gets a different claim, and mutual blocking left little for public investment.

mistakes: Treating caste as a cultural residue.
Reading an implementation problem without checking the federal bargain.
Assuming a pro-business state is pro-market.
Pushing services over transfers without noticing the structural bias in the politics.

recall.q: When did Bardhan publish his argument?
Which institutions mediate the federal bargain?
recall.a: The Finance Commission, the GST Council and party competition.

recall.q: Why do transfers beat services politically?
recall.a: A transfer is attributable, while a functioning school is diffuse and slow.

recall.q: Which country's settlements does Khan's work draw heavily on?
recall.a: Pakistan and Bangladesh.

recall.q: What does the reading list pair with Ostrom?
recall.a: Governing the Commons, for collective action.

notes.2: Eleven sections move from theory to practice. Sections 1 to 8 give you the ideas: classical roots, state and market, institutions, collective action, rents, development and settlements. Sections 9 to 11 turn them into a method and apply it to India and South Asia. Read the theory to sharpen how you read power.
notes.4: Economics asks whether something is efficient. Political economy adds **who wrote the rule** and who could stop a fix. Use the table as four questions to bring to any policy meeting. They separate a good recommendation from a feasible one, and the gap between them is where most reform effort is lost.
notes.5: Lasswell's line is the whole field in a sentence. Run the table as an exercise: a budget line decides who gets money, a subsidy decides which activity is cheap, a licence decides who may enter. Then add the question the slide recommends, **and who decided**, because the procedure reveals as much as the outcome.
notes.6: Technically sound reforms stall because they redistribute. Someone loses concentrated income, the losers are organised and the winners are dispersed. Replace 'lack of political will' with a question: **whose will, and what would change it?** Then assume everyone behaves rationally given their incentives and work out what those incentives are.
notes.7: This asymmetry explains most policy persistence. The losers are few, lose a lot each and are already organised. The winners are many, gain a little each and rarely mobilise. Remember the two tasks it implies: **organise the winners or compensate the losers**. A subsidy worth crores to twenty firms has one organised constituency.
notes.8: Keep explaining and judging apart. Positive questions ask what is and why, and normative questions ask what ought to be. The course is mostly positive, driven by a normative concern for who is left out. You can hold a strong position and still need an **accurate account of how things work** to act on it.
notes.9: Pick the level that matches your problem. Micro covers households and commons, meso covers sectors and regulators, macro covers national fiscal policy and global covers aid and trade rules. The same questions recur at each level. **A well-designed scheme can still fail because of incentives three levels up.**
notes.10: Treat political economy as a working tool for four jobs: diagnose why a reform stalls, map who can block, find a feasible entry point and anticipate what will undo your design. The slide flags a risk, that it can rationalise doing nothing. Section 9 addresses it, so **test the tool by whether it changes what you propose**.
notes.12: Until the late 19th century the discipline was called political economy, and the founders treated the state and the market as one subject with distribution at the centre. The renaming narrowed the lens. Today's revival returns to the founders' question: **how much is produced, for whom, and under what rules**.
notes.13: Smith's invisible hand has conditions. Self-interest serves society under real competition, free entry and an extensive market. The line to remember is about the butcher, the brewer and the baker. Where competition is absent, Smith's own analysis predicts the opposite outcome, so **the qualification matters as much as the metaphor**.
notes.14: Correct the caricature. Smith distrusted merchants' conspiracies, warned against monopoly, supported education and grounded markets in sympathy in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759). When someone invokes Smith against regulation, **quote his line** about people of the same trade ending their meetings in a conspiracy against the public.
notes.15: Ricardo's comparative advantage (1817) is the strongest case for trade, since both parties can gain. It says nothing about how the gains are shared or who bears the losses. That silence is where political economy enters. Gains are aggregate and losses concentrated, so **liberalisation is politically hard everywhere**.
notes.16: Marx made political economy a critique of capitalism. Profit comes from surplus value, so class conflict is structural. You do not need the labour theory of value to use his tools. The one to carry is row three: when an idea is dominant, **ask whose interest it serves** before asking whether it is true.
notes.17: Four Marxian tools travel without his political programme: material interests shape ideas, class structures conflict, accumulation drives concentration, and ideology can dress a particular interest as the common good. The first is the most portable. When an idea is taken as obvious, **ask who benefits from it being taken that way**.
notes.18: Use the table to see which thinker an argument stands on. A trade argument runs on Ricardo, a competition argument on Smith, and an analysis of who captures the gains on Marx. Knowing which one is a fast way to see what the argument assumes and **what it has left out**.
notes.20: The lazy debate sets market against state. The real question is which does what, here, since there is no market without a state to define property, enforce contracts and issue money. Work through the right-hand column: which rule enforced by whom, which failure is worse, and **which mix, designed how**.
notes.21: Learn the five failures with one example each: public goods, externalities, information gaps, monopoly power and missing markets. Each is a reason for state action and a guarantee of nothing. The political lesson is that **someone profits from every failure** and will resist the fix. Groundwater is the hardest case in the region.
notes.22: Memorise the five state roles: set rules, provide public goods, correct externalities, redistribute and stabilise. Each fails in a particular way, as the table shows. A state may be committed to all five and able to deliver two. Correcting an externality **imposes a concentrated cost on someone identifiable**.
notes.23: States fail too: capture, missing information, weak capacity and officials' own incentives. The mature question is comparative. Given that both fail, which failure is cheaper to fix here, for this problem? Ostrom later adds a **third option**, collective governance by users, which the market-or-state framing omits.
notes.24: Polanyi (1944) argued that creating a self-regulating market was a radical experiment. Land, labour and money are his three fictitious commodities because none is produced for sale. His claim is historical: societies resist because the consequences are unbearable. Learn the three and the **reason for each**.
notes.25: Embeddedness means economic activity sits inside social relations, norms and trust. In South Asia caste, kinship and credit relationships visibly structure who trades with whom. A design that assumes arm's-length strangers will meet the actual market, which **runs on obligation and information held in networks**.
notes.26: Learn the double movement as a two-step pattern: expansion of markets, then demands for protection. Backlash is a predictable counter-movement. The result is a mix of market and protection. Polanyi also noted that counter-movements can be illiberal, so **expect one and never assume it will be progressive**.
notes.27: Use the table to match expansion with counter-movement: 1991 liberalisation and rights-based guarantees, land markets and the Forest Rights Act, deregulated labour and the employment guarantee, the 2020 farm laws and their repeal. The practitioner lesson: a reform that removes protections **faster than society will bear** generates the backlash that reverses it.
notes.29: Four explanations for why some countries are rich: geography, culture, resources and institutions. The first three each have a standard objection in the table. The institutional answer dominates and is contested. For a practitioner the useful content is mid-level: **rules shape incentives, and incentives shape what people do**.
notes.30: North's definition is the one to quote: the humanly devised constraints, the rules of the game. Formal rules change by decision, quickly. Informal ones change slowly if at all. In South Asia the gap between the written rule and the operating rule is often the whole story, so **reforms that confuse the two fail predictably**.
notes.31: Keep rules and players apart. Institutions are the rules, and organisations are the players who exploit them and lobby to change them. Building a new agency rarely fixes a rule problem, and most capacity building targets the wrong layer. Players that prosper under the rules **defend them past their usefulness**.
notes.32: Acemoglu and Robinson sort institutions as inclusive or extractive. Inclusive ones reward innovation, allow entry, spread property rights and constrain the executive. Extractive ones funnel wealth to a narrow elite. The mechanism is creative destruction. Read the critique slide alongside it, since **the binary is contested**.
notes.33: Compare the two columns row by row: who participates, property rights, entry, incentive to invest, political power and long-run result. The authors say economic and political institutions reinforce each other, which makes extractive systems a trap. Most real configurations are mixed, so **identify the specific rule that blocks entry**.
notes.34: The scatter is illustrative. It shows higher institutional quality with higher income, and then asks which causes which. The left column shows a strong pattern and the right column shows an open causal question. For a practitioner the **mid-level claim** matters most: specific rules shape specific incentives, and those are observable locally.
notes.35: Four criticisms: a tautology risk, no theory of change, the China and East Asia counter-case, and country scores that hide variation. For a practitioner the second matters most. 'Just fix the institutions' is **advice and no plan**, which is why Section 8 on how rules change exists.
notes.37: Here is the puzzle: millions of consumers gain from a reform and a handful of producers lose, yet the producers win. The table shows why: a large stake each against a tiny one. Olson's insight is that shared interest usually does not produce action. This explains how **a policy that harms almost everyone a little survives**.
notes.38: Olson (1965) showed that rational people free-ride on shared benefits, so large groups under-provide their own collective goods. The logic is a chain: the benefit is non-excludable, contribution is costly, everyone reasons alike, the good is under-supplied. Awareness campaigns leave this untouched. **Only a change to the individual's incentive helps.**
notes.39: Small groups out-organise large ones because each share is large, defectors are visible and coordination is cheap. Large groups face tiny shares, unnoticed defection and costly coordination. The prediction is counter-intuitive and holds: **concentrated interests beat diffuse ones**. Mass organisations succeed through incentives, compulsion or federating small units.
notes.40: Learn the four fixes: selective incentives, coercion, small size or federation, and leadership. Effective movements such as unions, SEWA and farmer associations give members something only members get. Federation fits scale best: **small groups where monitoring works, nested into larger structures** where bargaining power lives, as in SHGs.
notes.41: Hardin (1968) described over-use of a shared finite resource, and falling water tables are the South Asian example. The table lists his assumptions and why each is often false. His model described open access with no governance and called it a commons. That **shaped policy for decades** towards privatisation and state takeover.
notes.42: Ostrom showed that communities do govern commons sustainably, without privatisation or top-down control, across forests, fisheries and irrigation systems. Her evidence was empirical and comparative, which is why it persuaded. She won the 2009 Nobel Prize. **Do not assume the only options are privatise or nationalise.**
notes.43: Memorise the eight design principles as questions to ask of any commons institution: who may use it, were the rules made here, can users change them, who monitors, are sanctions graduated, is there a fast forum, is self-organisation recognised, is governance nested. **Graduated sanctions** is the one most often missing.
notes.44: Test Ostrom's principles on South Asian cases. Joint Forest Management is the standard critique, because the forest department keeps rule-making authority, which violates the third principle. Water user associations risk boundaries and tail-end access, fishery cooperatives risk monitoring, and SHGs fit well. Match each to the **principle most at risk**.
notes.46: Rent is income above what is needed to keep a resource in use. Not all rent is bad, since a temporary innovation rent rewards risk. The danger is rent from artificial scarcity, such as a permit you must bribe for. The test is whether the rent is **conditional on performance**. Khan's learning rents complicate the usual verdict.
notes.47: Rent-seeking spends resources to capture an unearned share instead of creating wealth. Tullock's point is that the waste includes the effort spent competing for the transfer, as well as the transfer. The deeper cost: when returns are highest near the state, **the best talent goes there** and production loses it.
notes.48: The Licence Raj before 1991 is the textbook case of manufactured scarcity. Permits for capacity and imports made a licence worth a fortune, so firms competed for permits and ignored markets. The same logic operates today wherever discretion remains, such as **land, mining, spectrum and environmental clearance**.
notes.49: Corruption has types with different remedies. Petty bribes yield to removing discretion and digitisation, grand corruption needs transparency and competitive process, bureaucratic needs fewer approvals, and political needs party finance reform. One agency rarely addresses more than one. **Anti-corruption that ignores incentives just moves the bribe.**
notes.50: State capture is corruption moved upstream into writing the rules. It breaks no rule, so it is legal and enforcement is irrelevant. A captured state can look clean on paper. Look for procedural tells: **who drafted it, who was consulted and what the exemptions look like**.
notes.51: Elite capture can defeat flawless rules when local powerful groups control the list. Read the table as pairs of route and counter: read the list aloud publicly, publish objective criteria, publish entitlements, give grievances an independent route. The **public reading of beneficiary lists**, the core of the social audit, is the strongest single measure.
notes.52: Learn the difference. Patronage hands out jobs and contracts as favours for loyalty and is episodic. Clientelism is a standing exchange of goods for votes. Neither is simply bad: where rule-based entitlements are unreliable, a connection is a better bet. **Transparency and automatic entitlement** reduce clientelism by making the rule-based route work.
notes.53: Rank these instruments by how early they strike. Abolishing needless permits removes the scarcity itself, the first row and the most effective. Auctions and lotteries remove discretion, automatic entitlement removes the gatekeeper, transparency removes concealment and competition removes the monopoly rent. **Removing discretion works even if enforcers are dishonest.**
notes.55: After 1945 Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and later China transformed in a generation. The answer went well beyond free markets, to a particular relationship between state and capital. The finding to hold is that successful late developers had states that could **impose conditions on business and enforce them**.
notes.56: The developmental state steers sectors, disciplines firms and rests on a capable, relatively autonomous bureaucracy. Look at the tension in the first two rows: steering needs information, which means closeness, and disciplining needs autonomy, which means distance. You need to be **close enough to know and distant enough to say no**.
notes.57: Subsidy was a contract in East Asia, with cheap credit and protection tied to export targets and withdrawn from underperformers. Export targets worked because they were externally verifiable: a firm cannot lobby a foreign customer. The transferable principle: **any conditional subsidy needs a performance measure the recipient cannot manipulate**.
notes.58: Evans's balance has two failure modes. Too autonomous and the state is blind, too embedded and it is captured. South Asia has often had close ties without autonomy. More capacity and closer ties to business are each incomplete advice. In practice **rotation, merit recruitment and formal consultation** maintain the balance.
notes.59: The resource curse works through politics. Rents finance the state without taxing citizens, which reduces accountability. Add Dutch disease, volatility and conflict over the prize. The first row is the most important: **a state funded by rents does not need its citizens' consent**. Taxation builds accountability and rents remove the need for it.
notes.60: The chart is a schematic of the claim and uses no real data. As resource rents rise, governance quality falls. Note the exceptions, Norway and Botswana, which institutions explain since they were in place before the resource. The econometrics are contested and the **political mechanisms** are better established.
notes.61: Rodrik observed that manufacturing peaks at a much lower income in developing countries now and then declines. For South Asia that means services and informal work absorb labour leaving farms, while the high-productivity factory route that lifted East Asia narrows. Think of **a shorter escalator**. The causes are debated and the pattern is documented.
notes.62: South Asia's path is its own: services-led growth, a vast informal sector, strong democracy and a state often embedded without autonomy. The consequence in each row is political, such as entitlements that cannot run through employers. The fourth row is the sharpest contrast with East Asia: **close ties without reciprocal conditions**.
notes.64: Donors export independent regulators, merit bureaucracies and anti-corruption agencies, and they wither. The table shows why: each lacks a power base or threatens the coalition that funds politics. The explanation is that **institutions sit on a distribution of power**, so a new rule grafted onto unchanged power loses to the power. Section 10 names the pattern.
notes.65: Khan's move is to change the question from 'are these the right institutions?' to 'are they compatible with how power is distributed here?' The settlement decides which institutions are enforceable. Before designing, check compatibility: **who would have to accept a loss, and can they impose costs if they refuse?**
notes.66: Holding power is a group's capacity to benefit itself in conflict through organisation, wealth, numbers or disruption, and it need not match formal authority. A transport union or an association of intermediaries can block a reform. **Map holding power before you map the law** to make your stakeholder analysis predictive.
notes.67: Read the diagram left to right, then back along the arrow. Power shapes institutions, institutions shape outcomes and outcomes reshape power. The loop is slow, yet **the feedback arrow keeps the framework from being fatalistic**. Reform enters the loop and does not float above it, which is where effort can be directed.
notes.68: Informal rules often bind harder than the law: bribe norms override the fee schedule, caste hierarchy overrides equal access, understandings override merit rules. Design only for the formal rules and you are ambushed. **Map both**, by asking people who operate the system, in confidence, because none of it is written down.
notes.69: Read each row as predictable. A reform meets a settlement that conflicts with it, so the subsidy returns, postings stay political and the regulator is captured or starved. In each case the design is fine and the politics decide. The fourth row warns that digitisation often **relocates discretion** and leaves it in place.
notes.70: Khan's framework gives no counsel of despair. Work with the settlement: choose compatible reforms, shift the balance gradually, build the constituency first, take a small feasible win. Sometimes the win is to **channel rents to productive ends**. Critics warn of accommodating an unjust settlement, so name that trade-off.
notes.71: Diagnose which settlement you are in. Broad settlements have power shared, longer horizons and credible commitments, so rent recipients can be disciplined. Narrow or contested ones have short horizons and fragile reforms. Where it is contested, **expect short-horizon behaviour from everyone**, including officials. This is the bridge to PEA.
notes.73: PEA is a structured way to understand how power, interests and institutions shape a development problem. It produces a map, entry points and an account of why a reform stalls, with no prediction or guarantee. Its value depends on whether it **changes a design decision**. A PEA annexed to an unchanged document has done nothing.
notes.74: Early country-wide studies sat on shelves. The shift, associated with David Booth and ODI, was to problem-driven PEA that starts from one concrete problem. The sharper the statement, the more usable the answer: 'weak governance' produces nothing, while **'teachers absent three days a week here' produces a map**.
notes.75: Learn SIA as three layers: structures, institutions, actors. The third column of the table carries the practical value. Structures take decades, institutions years, and actors you engage now. Most programme effort should sit with actors, yet **most PEA reports spend most pages on structures**, the layer you cannot change.
notes.76: Structures are the slow stage: geography, demography, resource base, history, global position and social structure. You cannot change them in a project cycle, but ignoring them guarantees failure. Use them in reverse: a design that **requires a structural feature to be different** has found its own binding constraint.
notes.77: The institutions layer holds formal rules and the informal ones that override them. Pair each in the table: transparent tender against who is expected to win, merit posting against whose turn it is. The recurring finding is that the informal column dominates. Find it by **talking to operators off the record**.
notes.78: The actors layer is the operational one. For each actor establish what they want, what they gain or lose, how much power they hold and who they align with. The second row is the operative one. Stated positions are cheap, and **what an actor stands to lose predicts behaviour better**.
notes.79: TWP turns PEA from a report into a way of operating: read politics continuously, back local reformers, stay flexible and adapt as things shift. Its constraint is funders who can accept adaptive programming, and the idea itself is easy. The practical minimum is a **standing review agenda item**: what has changed politically.
notes.80: Use PEA as a lens and guard against four misuses: rationalising inaction, justifying the funder's plan, stale power maps and the analyst's own interest. The first is most common. A PEA that concludes only that the problem is political is **unfinished**, since the output must be a feasible next step, however small.
notes.82: Step one is naming the problem sharply, with a place, a group and an observable. Compare each vague problem with its sharp version in the table. Then follow the four-step chain: name, map, trace, find. Sharpening is usually **the highest-value hour in the exercise**, and teams skip it because the vague version already exists.
notes.83: Plot each actor by power and stance, then pick the tactic: champions get what they need, blockers are neutralised, compensated or avoided, allies get capacity and voice, and latent foes are watched. The table lists all four quadrants. Assess **informal holding power** and update the map, since power maps date quickly.
notes.84: Follow the incentives and ignore the org chart. A job description says serve citizens, while the incentives say please whoever controls your posting. If absent teachers are never sanctioned, absence is rational. The fourth row is the general form: where a target is reported and unverified, **the system rewards reporting**.
notes.85: Look for four kinds of entry point: aligned interests, a champion, a window and a small win. You rarely move the whole settlement. You look for the seam where a feasible push meets a willing ally and an open window. **Windows close**, so have the analysis ready before one opens.
notes.86: Recall Section 1: concentrated losers, diffuse winners. The task is to organise the winners with a visible stake, a vehicle, a champion and information. The last row is underrated, since diffuse losers often do not know they are losing. **Making a hidden cost visible** is often the first organising step.
notes.87: Best practice travels badly. Isomorphic mimicry, from Pritchett, Woolcock and Andrews, copies the form of an institution while its function never works: an agency exists and does nothing. The test is functional: **what does this body decide, and what happened the last time it decided something inconvenient?**
notes.88: PDIA is the constructive response to mimicry. Start from a locally felt problem, take small steps, learn fast from each and let solutions emerge, building authority as you go. It is closer to an engineering method than a policy. Its main obstacle is funding, since iteration is **hard to write into a fixed logframe**.
notes.89: The pensions case is illustrative, and it runs the whole course in five rows: problem, actors, incentives, entry point and champion. The value is in the last column. A finding that does not change what the programme does has not earned a place. Note that the **entry point is modest and specific**: a direct transfer and a public list.
notes.91: India is a paradox: a durable democracy with a vast, ambitious state that often delivers poorly. Hold democracy, caste, class, federalism and a large informal economy together. State-level variation is the analytical opportunity, because **the same national policy delivered differently across states** is a natural comparison.
notes.92: Bardhan (1984) said India's slow growth reflected a stand-off between three dominant proprietary classes: industrial capitalists, rich farmers and the professional elite. None could dominate and each could veto, so subsidies spread across all three and left little for public investment. It is **a settlement of mutual blocking**.
notes.93: Kohli's distinction is between pro-business and pro-market. Pro-business favours existing firms and profits, and pro-market favours competition and entry. India's shift from the 1980s moved toward the first. The consequence is that **a pro-business state protects incumbents**, which fits the persistence of concentrated sectors.
notes.94: India's federalism is a continuing bargain between the Centre and the states over taxes, transfers and authority, mediated by the Finance Commission, the GST Council and party competition. A first-order question is **which tier holds the money, the mandate and the staff** for your issue. Much of what looks like an implementation problem is a bargaining outcome.
notes.95: Caste operates as an economic institution. It structures access to land, credit and networks, education and the state itself. A PEA that treats actors as caste-blind will misread interests and power. Use caste and class together, since they cross-cut. **Who benefits is rarely separable from who belongs.**
notes.96: Recent decades brought rights and transfers: MGNREGA, the food and forest rights acts, DBT and free rations. Read them as a double movement and clientelism at once, since both readings are true. The last row is uncomfortable: a transfer is attributable while a functioning school is diffuse, so **competition favours transfers over services**.
notes.97: The wider region tests the frameworks. Pakistan and Bangladesh gave Khan's work much of its evidence, Bangladesh shows NGO-led delivery reshaping the state, and Sri Lanka and Nepal show cleavages shaping settlements. Common threads are informality, patronage, contested federalism and agrarian power. **Ground the theory in the specific country's distribution of power.**
notes.98: Use the reading list as a route into the sources. Acemoglu and Robinson cover institutions, Polanyi covers markets and society, Ostrom covers collective action, Bardhan covers India, and Khan and the ODI toolkits cover settlements and PEA. Pick the one that matches your **current problem** and read it first.
notes.99: Close with five questions you can ask of any policy problem without preparation. If you carry one, carry the third: **concentrated interests beat diffuse ones**, so ask who is organised here. The table pairs each takeaway with its question, so keep it beside your next stakeholder map.
